"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Linda Kenyon.
Flight delays and cancellations persist this morning as the nation's air travel industry
works through yesterday's severe weather.
But as NPR's John Stoleness reports, things are looking up.
The outlook is better today, as the nor'easter that caused so many headaches on Thanksgiving
has moved away from the East Coast.
The flight tracking website FlightAware reported a total of 462 flight cancellations in the
U.S. Thanksgiving Day, with over 2,800 delays.
Airports in Washington, D.C. and New York were most affected and were still seeing delays
on Friday.
The heaviest travel day of the Thanksgiving weekend will be on Sunday.
The Transportation Safety Administration projects they will screen more than 3 million passengers
at U.S. airports that day.
John Stoleness, NPR News.
The World Health Organization reports measles deaths around the world are at a historic
low.
But progress to eliminate the disease has been met with setbacks, as many countries
struggle to restore vaccination rates to pre-pandemic levels.
NPR's Maria Godoy has more.
The WHO says since 2000, vaccination efforts have helped reduce measles deaths worldwide
by 91 percent to 72,000 deaths last year.
But many countries have also experienced backsliding.
The U.S., Bolivia and Mexico all lost their measles elimination status last week.
Here's Dr. Kate O'Brien of the WHO.
I think this is the alarm bell for everybody around the world.
She says many people, including doctors, have not seen measles before.
But it is back, and the world is learning just how sick and just how dead measles can
make you.
In the U.S., states have reported more than a dozen measles-related deaths so far this
year.
Maria Godoy, NPR News.
The Iraqi government is closing border crossings run by Kurdish government forces.
NPR's Jane Araff reports it's a controversial move to take back control from the Kurdistan
region.
Iraqi state media says border forces have closed a crossing with Syria and another with
Iran in territory administered by the Kurdish regional government.
Kurds broke away from central government control under Saddam Hussein in 1992 and now administer
four majority Kurdish-Iraqi provinces, including border operations.
Earlier this week, the Iraqi prime minister announced that the federal oil ministry would
now run some of the biggest oil fields that are currently managed by Iraq's Kurdistan
regional government.
The government accuses Kurds of diverting oil proceeds.
They deny it.
The Kurdish leadership says it will not give up control of its borders or the oil fields.
Jane Araff, NPR News, Amman.
Kurdish leaders have rejected Baghdad's moves as unilateral, sparking protests in Erbil.
You're listening to NPR News.
Starting January 1st, work requirements are being added to Medicaid, the public health
insurance program for low-income people and the disabled.
As NPR's Selena Simmons-Duffin reports, last-minute changes to the rules and a rushed rollout
as people who rely on Medicaid confused and stressed.
Sarah Abend is 47 years old and lives in Detroit.
She's self-employed with a jewelry business.
She's currently trying to get re-enrolled in Medicaid.
She's worried about how the work requirements will affect her and whether her autoimmune
condition will mean she's exempt.
I guess it would mean some kind of a doctor's note because it's tricky with my case.
I rarely have pain with my condition.
It's the fatigue.
But exactly who will be exempt for medical reasons and how they will need to prove it
is still in flux.
States must put the new rules in place January 1st, but the Trump administration has said
they can choose to delay disenrolling people until next summer.
Selena Simmons-Duffin, NPR News, Washington.
This one is for the animal lovers out there.
A private zoo in Peru has introduced two baby meerkats born in Lima.
Meerkats are small mammals native to South Africa.
They dig underground burrows and often stand upright to watch for potential threats.
The Navi Fauna Zoo is home to 15 meerkats, eight of which have been born in Lima since
2025.
Navi Fauna says that the other seven arrived from their native Botswana in 2022 through
an exchange with other zoos.
I'm Lyndi Kenyon.
NPR News in Washington.
